Require
rē-kwīr´
v.t. (to demand as of right, to call for an account; rendering Hebrew darash, baqash, Greek aiteō, ekzēteō)
From Latin requirere, to seek again, to demand. In Scripture the verb belongs to God as Judge — He requires what He has a right to, and He requires it of named persons.

Biblical Definition

To require in Scripture is to demand by right, and God is nearly always the one requiring. Micah puts the whole moral law in the form of a question: “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” (Mic 6:8). He requires an account proportioned to what was given: “unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: and to whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more” (Luk 12:48) — privilege calculated as debt, not as advantage. He requires blood: after the flood He declares, “surely your blood of your lives will I require; at the hand of every beast will I require it, and at the hand of man” (Gen 9:5), the charter of human life's sanctity because man is made in God's image. And He requires the blood of the unwarned from the watchman who kept silent: “the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at thine hand” (Eze 3:18). What God requires, He will collect.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines require as to demand, to ask as of right and by authority; to claim as by right and authority; and to call to account for.

expand to see more

REQUIRE, v.t. To demand; to ask as of right and by authority.

2. To claim; to render necessary by an imperative statute.

3. To ask as a favor; to request.

4. To call to account for.

5. To make necessary; to need; to demand.

Key Scripture

Mic 6:8 — "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"

Luk 12:48 — "But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes. For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: and to whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more."

Gen 9:5 — "And surely your blood of your lives will I require; at the hand of every beast will I require it, and at the hand of man; at the hand of every man's brother will I require the life of man."

Eze 3:18 — "When I say unto the wicked, Thou shalt surely die; and thou givest him not warning, nor speakest to warn the wicked from his wicked way, to save his life; the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at thine hand."

Modern Corruption

Micah 6:8 has been detached from its context and made a summary of religion without atonement — a manageable ethic offered as an alternative to the sacrifice the same chapter assumes.

expand to see more

The verse is quoted as though it abolished the need for blood: God does not want offerings, only justice, mercy, and humility. But Micah 6 opens with the LORD pleading a covenant lawsuit against Israel, and the question in verse 6 is what a man shall bring — calves, thousands of rams, his firstborn for his transgression. The answer of verse 8 does not cancel sacrifice; it exposes sacrifice offered by men who trample the poor, exactly as Isaiah 1 does. Reduce the verse to a slogan and it becomes what it was never meant to be: a religion of decent conduct with no propitiation and no Saviour, which leaves the covenant lawsuit unanswered.

Luke 12:48 and Ezekiel 3:18 then close the exits. Much given means much required, so the well-taught church member stands under a heavier reckoning than the pagan, not a lighter one. And the watchman who saw the sword and said nothing is charged with the blood, which is the most sobering statement in Scripture about the cost of a comfortable silence. God requires; the only question is whether a man has a Substitute when the account is called.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew darash (H1875), to seek, enquire, require, and baqash (H1245), to seek or demand; Greek aiteō (G154) and ekzēteō (G1567), to demand or require of.

expand to see more

Hebrew darash (H1875) — to seek, enquire, require an account; “what doth the LORD require of thee” (Mic 6:8) and “will I require” (Gen 9:5).

Hebrew baqash (H1245) — to seek, demand; “his blood will I require at thine hand” (Eze 3:18).

Greek aiteō (G154) — to ask, demand; the passive of Luk 12:48, “of him shall be much required.”

Usage

"“What doth the LORD require of thee” — asked inside a covenant lawsuit, not outside one."

"“Unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required” — privilege reckoned as debt."

"“His blood will I require at thine hand” — the cost of a comfortable silence."
